{{Short description|Finest topology making some functions continuous}}
In [[general topology]] and related areas of [[mathematics]], the '''final topology'''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bourbaki |first1=Nicolas |author-link=Nicolas Bourbaki |title=General topology |date=1989 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=Berlin |isbn=978-3-540-64241-1 |page=32}}</ref> (or '''coinduced''',<ref>
{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kHPOBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA202 |title=Elements of Topology |last=Singh |first=Tej Bahadur |date=May 5, 2013 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=9781482215663 |access-date=July 21, 2020}}</ref> '''strong'''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Willard |first=Stephen |title=General topology |date=2004 |publisher=Dover Publications |isbn=978-0-486-43479-7 |location=Mineola, N.Y |pages=67}}</ref>, '''colimit''', or '''inductive'''<ref>{{cite book |last1=Császár |first1=Ákos |title=General topology |date=1978 |publisher=A. Hilger |location=Bristol [England] |isbn=0-85274-275-4 |page=317}}</ref> topology) on a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>X,</math> with respect to a family of functions from [[Topological space|topological spaces]] into <math>X,</math> is the [[finest topology]] on <math>X</math> that makes all those functions [[Continuous function (topology)|continuous]]. 

The [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient topology on a quotient space]] is a final topology, with respect to a single surjective function, namely the quotient map. The [[Disjoint union (topology)|disjoint union topology]] is the final topology with respect to the [[inclusion map]]s. The final topology is also the topology that every [[direct limit]] in the [[category of topological spaces]] is endowed with, and it is in the context of direct limits that the final topology often appears.  A topology is [[Coherent topology|coherent]] with some collection of [[Subspace topology|subspaces]] if and only if it is the final topology induced by the natural inclusions.  

The [[Duality (mathematics)|dual]] notion is the [[initial topology]], which for a given family of functions from a set <math>X</math> into topological spaces is the [[coarsest topology]] on <math>X</math> that makes those functions continuous. 

== Definition ==

Given a set <math>X</math> and an <math>I</math>-indexed family of [[topological space]]s <math>\left(Y_i, \upsilon_i\right)</math> with associated functions
<math display="block">f_i : Y_i \to X,</math>
the {{em|'''final topology''' on <math>X</math> induced by the family of functions <math>\mathcal{F} := \left\{ f_i : i \in I \right\}</math>}} is the [[finest topology]] <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> on <math>X</math> such that
<math display="block">f_i : \left(Y_i, \upsilon_i\right) \to \left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right)</math>

is [[continuous (topology)|continuous]] for each <math>i\in I</math>. The final topology always exists, and is unique.

Explicitly, the final topology may be described as follows:
:a subset <math>U</math> of <math>X</math> is open in the final topology <math>\left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right)</math> (that is, <math>U \in \tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math>) [[if and only if]] <math>f_i^{-1}(U)</math> is open in <math>\left(Y_i, \upsilon_i\right)</math> for each <math>i\in I</math>.

The closed subsets have an analogous characterization:
:a subset <math>C</math> of <math>X</math> is closed in the final topology <math>\left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right)</math> if and only if <math>f_i^{-1}(C)</math> is closed in <math>\left(Y_i, \upsilon_i\right)</math> for each <math>i\in I</math>.

The family <math>\mathcal{F}</math> of functions that induces the final topology on <math>X</math> is usually a ''set'' of functions.  But the same construction can be performed if <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is a [[proper class]] of functions, and the result is still well-defined in [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]].  In that case there is always a subfamily <math>\mathcal{G}</math> of <math>\mathcal{F}</math> with <math>\mathcal{G}</math> a set, such that the final topologies on <math>X</math> induced by <math>\mathcal{F}</math> and by <math>\mathcal{G}</math> coincide.  For more on this, see for example the discussion here.<ref>{{cite web |title=Set theoretic issues in the definition of k-space or final topology wrt a proper class of functions |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4639381 |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange}}</ref>  As an example, a commonly used variant of the notion of [[compactly generated space]] is defined as the final topology with respect to a proper class of functions.{{sfn|Brown|2006|loc=Section 5.9, p. 182}}

== Examples ==

The important special case where the family of maps <math>\mathcal{F}</math> consists of a single surjective map can be completely characterized using the notion of [[quotient map (topology)|quotient map]]. A surjective function <math>f : (Y, \upsilon) \to \left(X, \tau\right)</math> between topological spaces is a quotient map if and only if the topology  <math>\tau</math> on <math>X</math> coincides with the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> induced by the family <math>\mathcal{F}=\{f\}</math>. In particular: the [[quotient topology]] is the final topology on the quotient space induced by the [[quotient map (topology)|quotient map]]. 

The final topology on a set <math>X</math> induced by a family of <math>X</math>-valued maps can be viewed as a far reaching generalization of the quotient topology, where multiple maps may be used instead of just one and where these maps are not required to be surjections. 

Given topological spaces <math>X_i</math>, the [[disjoint union (topology)|disjoint union topology]] on the [[disjoint union]] <math>\coprod_i X_i</math> is the final topology on the disjoint union induced by the natural injections.

Given a [[Family of sets|family]] of topologies <math>\left(\tau_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> on a fixed set <math>X,</math> the final topology on <math>X</math> with respect to the identity maps <math>\operatorname{id}_{\tau_i} : \left(X, \tau_i\right) \to X</math> as <math>i</math> ranges over <math>I,</math> call it <math>\tau,</math> is the [[infimum]] (or meet) of these topologies <math>\left(\tau_i\right)_{i \in I}</math> in the [[lattice of topologies]] on <math>X.</math> That is, the final topology <math>\tau</math> is equal to the [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]] <math display="inline">\tau = \bigcap_{i \in I} \tau_i.</math>

Given a topological space <math>(X,\tau)</math> and a family <math>\mathcal C=\{ C_i : i\in I\}</math> of subsets of <math>X</math> each having the [[subspace topology]], the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal C}</math> induced by all the inclusion maps of the <math>C_i</math> into <math>X</math> is [[Comparison of topologies|finer]] than (or equal to) the original topology <math>\tau</math> on <math>X.</math>  The space <math>X</math> is called [[coherent (topology)|coherent]] with the family <math>\mathcal C</math> of subspaces if the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal C}</math> coincides with the original topology <math>\tau.</math>  In that case, a subset <math>U\subseteq X</math> will be open in <math>X</math> exactly when the intersection <math>U\cap C_i</math> is open in <math>C_i</math> for each <math>i\in I.</math>  (See the [[coherent topology]] article for more details on this notion and more examples.)  As a particular case, one of the notions of [[compactly generated space]] can be characterized as a certain coherent topology.

The [[direct limit]] of any direct system of spaces and continuous maps is the set-theoretic direct limit together with the final topology determined by the canonical morphisms. 
Explicitly, this means that if <math>\operatorname{Sys}_Y = \left(Y_i, f_{ji}, I\right)</math> is a direct system in the [[Category of topological spaces|category '''Top''' of topological spaces]] and if <math>\left(X, \left(f_i\right)_{i \in I}\right)</math> is a direct limit of <math>\operatorname{Sys}_Y</math> in the [[Category of sets|category '''Set''' of all sets]], then by endowing <math>X</math> with the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> induced by <math>\mathcal{F} := \left\{ f_i : i \in I \right\},</math> <math>\left(\left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right), \left(f_i\right)_{i \in I}\right)</math> becomes the direct limit of <math>\operatorname{Sys}_Y</math> in the category '''Top'''. 

The [[étalé space]] of a sheaf is topologized by a final topology. 

A [[first-countable]] [[Hausdorff space]] <math>(X, \tau)</math> is [[locally path-connected]] if and only if <math>\tau</math> is equal to the final topology on <math>X</math> induced by the set <math>C\left([0, 1]; X\right)</math> of all continuous maps <math>[0, 1] \to (X, \tau),</math> where any such map is called a [[Path (mathematics)|path]] in <math>(X, \tau).</math>

If a Hausdorff [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] [[topological vector space]] <math>(X, \tau)</math> is a [[Fréchet-Urysohn space]] then <math>\tau</math> is equal to the final topology on <math>X</math> induced by the set <math>\operatorname{Arc}\left([0, 1]; X\right)</math> of all [[Arc (topology)|arcs]] in <math>(X, \tau),</math> which by definition are continuous [[Path (mathematics)|paths]] <math>[0, 1] \to (X, \tau)</math> that are also [[topological embedding]]s.

== Properties ==

=== Characterization via continuous maps ===
Given functions <math>f_i : Y_i \to X,</math> from topological spaces <math>Y_i</math> to the set <math>X</math>, the final topology on <math>X</math> with respect to these functions <math>f_i</math> satisfies the following property:
:a function <math>g</math> from <math>X</math> to some space <math>Z</math> is continuous if and only if <math>g \circ f_i</math> is continuous for each <math>i \in I.</math>
[[Image:FinalTopology-01.png|center|Characteristic property of the final topology]]

This property characterizes the final topology in the sense that if a topology on <math>X</math> satisfies the property above for all spaces <math>Z</math> and all functions <math>g:X\to Z</math>, then the topology on <math>X</math> is the final topology with respect to the <math>f_i.</math>

=== Behavior under composition ===
Suppose <math>\mathcal{F} := \left\{ f_i:Y_i \to X \mid i \in I \right\}</math> is a family of maps, and for every <math>i \in I,</math> the topology <math>\upsilon_i</math> on <math>Y_i</math> is the final topology induced by some family <math>\mathcal{G}_i</math> of maps valued in <math>Y_i</math>. Then the final topology on <math>X</math> induced by <math>\mathcal{F}</math> is equal to the final topology on <math>X</math> induced by the maps <math>\left\{ f_i \circ g ~:~ i \in I \text{ and } g \in \cal G_i \right\}.</math> 

As a consequence: if <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> is the final topology on <math>X</math> induced by the family <math>\mathcal{F} := \left\{ f_i : i \in I \right\}</math> and if <math>\pi : X \to (S, \sigma)</math> is any [[surjective map]] valued in some topological space <math>(S, \sigma),</math> then <math>\pi : \left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right) \to (S, \sigma)</math> is a [[quotient map (topology)|quotient map]] if and only if <math>(S, \sigma)</math> has the final topology induced by the maps <math>\left\{ \pi \circ f_i ~:~ i \in I \right\}.</math> 

By the [[universal property]] of the [[disjoint union topology]] we know that given any family of continuous maps <math>f_i : Y_i \to X,</math> there is a unique continuous map
<math display="block">f : \coprod_i Y_i \to X</math>
that is compatible with the natural injections.
If the family of maps <math>f_i</math> {{em|covers}} <math>X</math> (i.e. each <math>x \in X</math> lies in the image of some <math>f_i</math>) then the map <math>f</math> will be a [[quotient map (topology)|quotient map]] if and only if <math>X</math> has the final topology induced by the maps <math>f_i.</math>

===Effects of changing the family of maps===

Throughout, let <math>\mathcal{F} := \left\{ f_i : i \in I \right\}</math> be a family of <math>X</math>-valued maps with each map being of the form <math>f_i : \left(Y_i, \upsilon_i\right) \to X</math> and let <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> denote the final topology on <math>X</math> induced by <math>\mathcal{F}.</math> 
The definition of the final topology guarantees that for every index <math>i,</math> the map <math>f_i : \left(Y_i, \upsilon_i\right) \to \left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right)</math> is [[Continuous function (topology)|continuous]]. 

For any subset <math>\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{F},</math> the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal{S}}</math> on <math>X</math> will be [[Comparison of topologies|{{em|finer}} than]] (and possibly equal to) the topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math>; that is, <math>\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{F}</math> implies <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}} \subseteq \tau_{\mathcal{S}},</math> where set equality might hold even if <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is a [[Subset|proper subset]] of <math>\mathcal{F}.</math> 

If <math>\tau</math> is any topology on <math>X</math> such that <math>\tau \neq \tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> and <math>f_i : \left(Y_i, \upsilon_i\right) \to (X, \tau)</math> is continuous for every index <math>i \in I,</math> then <math>\tau</math> must be [[Comparison of topologies|{{em|strictly coarser}}]] than <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> (meaning that <math>\tau \subseteq \tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> and <math>\tau \neq \tau_{\mathcal{F}};</math> this will be written <math>\tau \subsetneq \tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math>) and moreover, for any subset <math>\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{F}</math> the topology <math>\tau</math> will also be {{em|strictly coarser}} than the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal{S}}</math> that <math>\mathcal{S}</math> induces on <math>X</math> (because <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}} \subseteq \tau_{\mathcal{S}}</math>); that is, <math>\tau \subsetneq \tau_{\mathcal{S}}.</math> 

Suppose that in addition, <math>\mathcal{G} := \left\{g_a : a \in A\right\}</math> is an <math>A</math>-indexed family of <math>X</math>-valued maps <math>g_a : Z_a \to X</math> whose domains are topological spaces <math>\left(Z_a, \zeta_a\right).</math> 
If every <math>g_a : \left(Z_a, \zeta_a\right) \to \left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right)</math> is continuous then adding these maps to the family <math>\mathcal{F}</math> will {{em|not}} change the final topology on <math>X;</math> that is, <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{G}} = \tau_{\mathcal{F}}.</math> 
Explicitly, this means that the final topology on <math>X</math> induced by the "extended family" <math>\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{G}</math> is equal to the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> induced by the original family <math>\mathcal{F} = \left\{ f_i : i \in I \right\}.</math> 
However, had there instead existed even just one map <math>g_{a_0}</math> such that <math>g_{a_0} : \left(Z_{a_0}, \zeta_{a_0}\right) \to \left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right)</math> was {{em|not}} continuous, then the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{G}}</math> on <math>X</math> induced by the "extended family" <math>\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{G}</math> would necessarily be [[Comparison of topologies|{{em|strictly coarser}}]] than the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> induced by <math>\mathcal{F};</math> that is, <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{G}} \subsetneq \tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> (see this footnote<ref group="note">By definition, the map <math>g_{a_0} : \left(Z_{a_0}, \zeta_{a_0}\right) \to \left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right)</math> not being continuous means that there exists at least one open set <math>U \in \tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> such that <math>g_{a_0}^{-1}(U)</math> is not open in <math>\left(Z_{a_0}, \zeta_{a_0}\right).</math> In contrast, by definition of the final topology <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F} \cup \{g_{a_0}\}},</math> the map <math>g_{a_0} : \left(Z_{a_0}, \zeta_{a_0}\right) \to \left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F} \cup \{g_{a_0}\}}\right)</math> {{em|must}} be continuous. So the reason why <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F} \cup \mathcal{G}}</math> must be strictly coarser, rather than strictly finer, than <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> is because the failure of the map <math>g_{a_0} : \left(Z_{a_0}, \zeta_{a_0}\right) \to \left(X, \tau_{\mathcal{F}}\right)</math> to be continuous necessitates that one or more open subsets of <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> must be "removed" in order for <math>g_{a_0}</math> to become continuous. Thus <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F} \cup \{g_{a_0}\}}</math> is just <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}</math> but some open sets "removed" from <math>\tau_{\mathcal{F}}.</math></ref> for an explanation).

== Final topology on the direct limit of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces ==

Let 
<math display="block">\R^{\infty} ~:=~ \left\{ \left(x_1, x_2, \ldots\right) \in \R^{\N} ~:~ \text{ all but finitely many } x_i \text{ are equal to } 0 \right\},</math>
denote the '''{{em|[[space of finite sequences]]}}''', where <math>\R^{\N}</math> denotes the [[space of all real sequences]]. 
For every [[natural number]] <math>n \in \N,</math> let <math>\R^n</math> denote the usual [[Euclidean space]] endowed with the [[Euclidean topology]] and let <math>\operatorname{In}_{\R^n} : \R^n \to \R^{\infty}</math> denote the [[inclusion map]] defined by <math>\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\left(x_1, \ldots, x_n\right) := \left(x_1, \ldots, x_n, 0, 0, \ldots\right)</math> so that its [[Image (mathematics)|image]] is
<math display="block">\operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right) 
= \left\{ \left(x_1, \ldots, x_n, 0, 0, \ldots\right) ~:~ x_1, \ldots, x_n \in \R \right\} 
= \R^n \times \left\{ (0, 0, \ldots) \right\}</math>
and consequently,
<math display="block">\R^{\infty} = \bigcup_{n \in \N} \operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right).</math> 

Endow the set <math>\R^{\infty}</math> with the final topology <math>\tau^{\infty}</math> induced by the family <math>\mathcal{F} := \left\{ \; \operatorname{In}_{\R^n} ~:~ n \in \N \; \right\}</math> of all inclusion maps. 
With this topology, <math>\R^{\infty}</math> becomes a [[Complete topological vector space|complete]] [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] [[Sequential space|sequential]] [[topological vector space]] that is {{em|not}} a [[Fréchet–Urysohn space]]. 
The topology <math>\tau^{\infty}</math> is [[Comparison of topologies|strictly finer]] than the [[subspace topology]] induced on <math>\R^{\infty}</math> by <math>\R^{\N},</math> where <math>\R^{\N}</math> is endowed with its usual [[product topology]]. 
Endow the image <math>\operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right)</math> with the final topology induced on it by the [[bijection]] <math>\operatorname{In}_{\R^n} : \R^n \to \operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right);</math> that is, it is endowed with the Euclidean topology transferred to it from <math>\R^n</math> via <math>\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}.</math> 
This topology on <math>\operatorname{Im} \left( \operatorname{In}_{\R^n} \right)</math> is equal to the subspace topology induced on it by <math>\left(\R^{\infty}, \tau^{\infty}\right).</math> 
A subset <math>S \subseteq \R^{\infty}</math> is open (respectively, closed) in <math>\left(\R^{\infty}, \tau^{\infty}\right)</math> if and only if for every <math>n \in \N,</math> the set <math>S \cap \operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right)</math> is an open (respectively, closed) subset of <math>\operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right).</math> 
The topology <math>\tau^{\infty}</math> is coherent with the family of subspaces <math>\mathbb{S} := \left\{ \; \operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right) ~:~ n \in \N \; \right\}.</math> 
This makes <math>\left(\R^{\infty}, \tau^{\infty}\right)</math> into an [[LB-space]]. 
Consequently, if <math>v \in \R^{\infty}</math> and <math>v_{\bull}</math> is a sequence in <math>\R^{\infty}</math> then <math>v_{\bull} \to v</math> in <math>\left(\R^{\infty}, \tau^{\infty}\right)</math> if and only if there exists some <math>n \in \N</math> such that both <math>v</math> and <math>v_{\bull}</math> are contained in <math>\operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right)</math> and <math>v_{\bull} \to v</math> in <math>\operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right).</math> 

Often, for every <math>n \in \N,</math> the inclusion map <math>\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}</math> is used to identify <math>\R^n</math> with its image <math>\operatorname{Im} \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right)</math> in <math>\R^{\infty};</math> explicitly, the elements <math>\left( x_1, \ldots, x_n \right) \in \R^n</math> and <math>\left(x_1, \ldots, x_n, 0, 0, 0, \ldots\right)</math> are identified together. 
Under this identification, <math>\left(\left(\R^{\infty}, \tau^{\infty}\right), \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^n}\right)_{n \in \N}\right)</math> becomes a [[direct limit]] of the direct system <math>\left(\left(\R^n\right)_{n \in \N}, \left(\operatorname{In}_{\R^m}^{\R^n}\right)_{m \leq n \text{ in } \N}, \N\right),</math> where for every <math>m \leq n,</math> the map <math>\operatorname{In}_{\R^m}^{\R^n} : \R^m \to \R^n</math> is the inclusion map defined by <math>\operatorname{In}_{\R^m}^{\R^n}\left(x_1, \ldots, x_m\right) := \left(x_1, \ldots, x_m, 0, \ldots, 0\right),</math> where there are <math>n - m</math> trailing zeros.

== Categorical description ==

In the language of [[category theory]], the final topology construction can be described as follows. Let <math>Y</math> be a [[functor]] from a [[discrete category]] <math>J</math> to the [[category of topological spaces]] '''Top''' that selects the spaces <math>Y_i</math> for <math>i \in J.</math> Let <math>\Delta</math> be the [[diagonal functor]] from '''Top''' to the [[functor category]] '''Top'''<sup>''J''</sup> (this functor sends each space <math>X</math> to the constant functor to <math>X</math>). The [[comma category]] <math>(Y \,\downarrow\, \Delta)</math> is then the [[category of co-cones]] from <math>Y,</math> i.e. objects in <math>(Y \,\downarrow\, \Delta)</math> are pairs <math>(X, f)</math> where <math>f = (f_i : Y_i \to X)_{i \in J}</math> is a family of continuous maps to <math>X.</math> If <math>U</math> is the [[forgetful functor]] from '''Top''' to '''Set''' and Δ&prime; is the diagonal functor from '''Set''' to '''Set'''<sup>''J''</sup> then the comma category <math>\left(UY \,\downarrow\, \Delta^{\prime}\right)</math> is the category of all co-cones from <math>UY.</math> The final topology construction can then be described as a functor from <math>\left(UY \,\downarrow\, \Delta^{\prime}\right)</math> to <math>(Y \,\downarrow\, \Delta).</math> This functor is [[Adjoint functors|left adjoint]] to the corresponding forgetful functor.
